members: Build habits around the kind of person you want to be, not only the outcomes you want.
Choose carefully what to care about, because attention and energy are limited.
Accept that life involves constant problems and look for problems you enjoy solving.
Stop trying to feel good all the time and accept negative emotions as normal.
Take responsibility for everything that happens to you, even when it is not your fault.
Be willing to be wrong and test your beliefs about yourself and the world.
Choose good values: those based on things you control, such as honesty, curiosity, and humility.
Learn to say no and set boundaries in relationships.
Commit to people, projects, and choices rather than keeping every option open.
Do not see yourself as exceptional; accept being ordinary and work on mundane tasks.
Stand up straight with your shoulders back, carrying yourself with confidence.
Treat yourself as someone you are responsible for helping, as you would a person you care for.
Befriend people who want the best for you, and drop those who drag you down.
Compare yourself to who you were yesterday, not to other people.
Put your own life in order before criticizing the world.
Pet a cat when you encounter one, and notice the small good things in life.
Reject the idea that past events or trauma determine your present; choose your actions based on present goals.
Accept that you can change in this moment by choosing a new lifestyle.
Stop comparing yourself to others and see differences as equal, not as superior or inferior.
Separate your tasks from other people's tasks and do not interfere in theirs.
Treat others as equals and build horizontal relationships.
Contribute to others without needing gratitude, because the feeling of contribution is itself happiness.
Accept yourself as you are and focus on using what you have, not on what you lack.
Be willing to be vulnerable; accept that uncertainty, risk, and emotional exposure are part of living fully.
Reject the belief that vulnerability is weakness.
Resist the culture of scarcity, the feeling of never being enough, and practice recognizing what is enough.
Let go of perfectionism and the fear of what others think.
Do not numb discomfort with busyness, substances, or other buffers.
Lead by encouraging vulnerability, honest feedback, and curiosity in organizations and classrooms.
Accept that you are worthy of love and belonging as you are.
Embrace challenges instead of avoiding them to look smart.
Treat setbacks and failure as information and chances to learn, not as a verdict on your worth.
Be inspired by others' success instead of feeling threatened.
Coach and lead others by encouraging development and teamwork, not by building a culture of genius.
In relationships, see partners as able to grow and work on problems together; do not blame or belittle.
Do not use labels such as gifted or failure for yourself or others.
Change your mindset gradually by noticing your fixed-mindset voice and choosing a growth response.
Pursue less but better: focus on the vital few things and deliberately drop the trivial many.
Know that you can choose what to do; you are not forced to accept every demand.
Aim for tiny improvements each day, since small changes compound into large results over time.
Focus on systems and daily processes rather than on goals alone.
Make a desired habit obvious by noticing cues and writing down a specific plan for when and where you will do it.
Stack a new habit onto an existing routine so the old one triggers the new one.
Redesign your surroundings so good cues are visible and bad cues are hidden.
Make habits attractive by pairing them with something you enjoy and joining groups where the habit is normal.
Make habits easy by reducing steps and starting with a version that takes about 2 minutes.
Make good habits satisfying with immediate rewards and track them visibly, for example with a habit tracker.
Never miss twice in a row; if you skip a day, get back on track right away.
Make bad habits invisible, unattractive, difficult, and unsatisfying, reversing the rules for good ones.
Pick activities that suit your strengths and personality, and keep working at the edge of your ability.
Review your habits regularly and avoid tying your identity too rigidly to one role.
Act first and let motivation follow, instead of waiting to feel inspired.
Embrace boredom and train focus; do not switch to distraction at every brief pause.
Practice productive meditation: focus on one problem while doing physical activity such as walking.
Memorize or concentrate on structured material to improve your concentration.
Apply the 80/20 rule: find the few tasks and customers that produce most results and drop the rest.
Limit work to the essentials, setting tight deadlines and low-information routines.
Do not wait for the perfect time; take action and improve as you go.
Value effort as the path to mastery, not as a sign of lack of ability.
In sports and business, focus on process and improvement, not on being a natural.
Make time to explore and think; give yourself space for reflection and play.
Escape to a quiet place regularly to think and decide what is essential.
Remove obstacles to the essential, finding the biggest constraint and clearing it.
Start small and reward progress, aiming for small wins instead of grand launches.
Build routines that make essentials automatic, and protect the assets of body and sleep.
Be present in the moment and focus on what is important right now.
Do not let your children behave in ways that make others dislike them.
Do not bother children while they are skating, letting them take risks and develop competence.
Do not praise or rebuke others; encourage them instead to build their sense of contribution.
Parent by modeling worthiness and connection, not perfection, and let children see you being imperfect.
Adopt a growth mindset: believe abilities can be developed through effort, strategy, and help.
Seek feedback and learn from criticism instead of getting defensive.
Praise children for effort, strategies, and persistence rather than for intelligence or talent.
Think about your own mortality to put your concerns in perspective.
Pursue what is meaningful, not what is expedient.
Live earnestly in the present moment, treating life as a series of dancing moments, not a path to a goal.
Define what you want and fear, and set goals to build a lifestyle you actually want instead of postponing life to retirement.
Fill the time you free up with learning, experiences, and service, not more work.
